title: House Robber
statement:
A row of houses holds some cash: `nums[i]` is the amount in house `i`. You want to collect as much as possible, but neighbouring houses share an alarm, so you may never take from **two adjacent houses**.

Return the largest total you can collect. Taking nothing is allowed, so the answer is never negative.

target.note: The plain recursion rob(i) = max(rob(i+1), nums[i] + rob(i+2)) is exponential and won't finish even the smallest benchmark. Memoizing it gives O(n); the two-variable loop gives O(n) time and O(1) space.

hints: Look only at the last house. Either you take it or you don't. If you take it, what does that rule out, and what smaller problem is left in each case?

Let best(i) be the most you can collect from the first i houses. Then best(i) = max(best(i-1), best(i-2) + nums[i-1]). The naive recursion recomputes the same best(j) exponentially often; storing each answer once makes it linear.

Iterate left to right keeping just two numbers: the best total for the prefix ending one house back, and two houses back. For each house the new best is max(oneBack, twoBack + nums[i]); then shift the two variables. That is O(n) time and O(1) space.
followups: The houses are arranged in a circle, so the first and last are neighbours. How do you reuse this solution?
Return which houses to take, not just the total. What extra information do you have to keep?
The houses form a binary tree and you can't take a parent and its child together. What does each subtree need to report to its parent?
explain: Each house is a take-or-skip decision, and taking house i forbids house i-1. So the best total for the first i houses is max(best(i-1), best(i-2) + nums[i-1]): either skip house i, or take it on top of the best answer that ends two houses back. Written as plain recursion this branches twice per house and recomputes the same prefixes over and over, roughly φ^n calls. Every subproblem is just a prefix length, so there are only n of them; memoizing or filling a table bottom-up makes it O(n). Since each step only looks two back, two variables are enough, giving O(1) space. With values ≤ 10^4 and n ≤ 10^5 the total stays under 10^9, so int is safe here; use long if the bounds grow. This 'include the current item, or carry forward the best without it' recurrence is the template for a whole family of 1-D DP problems.
